composition.intent: How to build a screen this ledger has no component for. DESIGN_LANGUAGE.md section 6 holds the same subject as relations that survive a change of theme; these are the bindings for this theme.
composition.accentBudget: The budget is AREA MULTIPLIED BY CHROMA, not "is it saturated". One solid accent fill per screen for the primary action, plus small solid indicators, which are the cheapest accent there is. A washed accent is for independent, scattered items — a filter chip — and never for a closed contiguous set, where position already carries the state. Never on a heading, a rule, or a decorative tag.
donts: Never a third surface level. With elevation: borders a level is carried by a hairline, and a third would have to be a second hairline, which is not a level.
Never tint a heading for emphasis — hierarchy is size and weight.
Never separate surfaces with a shadow. That decision was made in question 7 and spending it twice separates the same page two ways.

A rail spends no rung. It is separated by a hairline, never by a tone of its own — a nav is already distinguishable by position, density and typography, and rung three belongs to the quiet fill that badges, chips and resting secondary actions are made of. Reversal recorded: this ledger forbade a rail outright until 0.9.0, on the argument that it would be the application announcing itself. The product acquired four destinations, and four destinations with nowhere to live is a worse answer than a quiet rail.
composition.frame: application frame — a persistent rail on the left, the reading column in the middle, an aside on the right. The rail and the aside are chrome at fixed widths; the measure stays on the middle column, which is the whole reason it is named.
composition.disclosure: progressive — secondary actions sit behind the item they act on rather than in every row; filters open rather than persist.
composition.iconPolicy: Icons lead their labels. Alone only in a repeated toolbar, and never on a destructive action.

forms.saving: draft saved automatically; the recipe enters the notebook on an explicit review-and-save
forms.confirmations: a modal, because deleting a saved recipe cannot be undone
forms.destructive: one confirmation step, never a typed name — the data is recoverable from the draft

button.intent: A control that performs an action. If it navigates to a URL, it is an anchor and nothing here applies.
button.namespaceNote: Every `btn-*` class in CoreUI is a variant, so the wide lookahead is right here — it is the exception among the components in this file. `btn-group`, `btn-toolbar` and `btn-close` are a container, a container and an icon, so the lookahead marks where this component's authority ends.

primary.intent: The action a screen exists for: save the recipe, start cooking mode.
dos: One per screen. The accent is a pen, not a highlighter.
donts: Never two side by side — a screen with two main actions has two jobs.

trajectory.when: never, unless the shape stops fitting
trajectory.why: Nothing is lost by staying raw. CoreUI's button geometry already matches the archetype once the entry sets radius, weight and control height, so promotion would buy shape this product already has. Recorded so the next reader knows it was considered rather than missed.

secondary.intent: A supporting action beside the primary one: cancel, back, dismiss.
secondary.notes: RUNG 3, and it was the solid neutral until 0.9.0 — rung 9, with inverted ink, which is a small dark button standing beside the primary and competing with it. The cause was structural rather than a slip: layer 3 named no secondary button, so the adapter generated `.btn-secondary` from the `neutral` theme role like any other colour, and `neutral` is the ONE SOLID neutral. claude-4.md puts the resting fill of a neutral secondary on rung 3, carrying ordinary dark ink — the same quiet fill a badge and a chip are made of — and adds the rule for when it feels too faint: raise the rung, never add an outline.
dos: Beside the primary, at most one or two per region.
donts: Never outlined instead. Filled and outlined on one screen are the same rank twice and invent a fourth level.

danger.intent: Reaching for something hard to undo from a page where it is not the main business: the delete beside a recipe.
dos: At the far edge of an action row, never beside the primary.
danger.notes: GHOST IN THE DANGER INK, and it has now been solid, then outlined, then this. The solid version put a second full-strength fill on a page that already had one and read as more important than the save. The outline fixed that and broke something else: claude-4.md — "ter secundário preenchido E contornado na mesma tela cria um quarto nível de hierarquia que ninguém pediu". An outline is not a rank; it is the SAME rank as the filled secondary reached by a different mechanism, and a product picks one and stays with it. This one is filled, so nothing in it is outlined. What was left was to notice that destructive is an INTENT laid over a rank rather than a rank of its own — and on this page the delete is tertiary: not what the screen is for, pushed to the far edge, with a confirmation in front of it.
donts: Never solid outside its own confirmation — see `danger-confirm`.
Never outlined. This product has no outlined buttons at all, by the rule above.

quiet.intent: A tertiary action INSIDE FLOWING TEXT, where even a ghost button would be a box interrupting a sentence: edit a step, remove an ingredient row.
quiet.notes: Distinct from `tertiary`, and the difference is the surroundings rather than the emphasis. `btn-link` is shaped like the prose it sits in; `btn-ghost` is shaped like the buttons it sits beside. Using either in the other place is what makes an action bar look ragged or a paragraph look interrupted.

status-coloured.intent: A button carrying a status colour to suggest an outcome.
status-coloured.reason: A status colour reports an outcome that has happened; a button proposes an action that has not. A green Save reads as already saved. This product also adapts its status colours down so they do not compete with a photograph of food, which makes them weaker as buttons than the accent already is.

absolute-palette.intent: A button coloured by a fixed palette name rather than a theme role.
absolute-palette.reason: `light` and `dark` are palette entries, not theme roles. They do not invert, so a light button stays light on the dark theme. This is a measured fact about the library rather than a matter of taste.

tertiary.intent: The third rank in a row of buttons: an action that is available and is not being suggested. Print, duplicate, export.
tertiary.notes: The ladder of prominence, and the page had no example of its bottom rung until 0.9.0 — which is its own finding, because a rank nobody renders is a rank nobody designed. `btn-ghost` carries no border at rest AND none on hover, which is claude-4.md's row for the tertiary button: it rises to a rung 3 fill on hover instead. That is the state rule for the whole system — hover and active change RUNG, never TREATMENT. A ghost that gained a border on hover would be changing family mid-gesture.
dos: Third in a row, after the primary and the secondary.
donts: Never alone as the only action in a region — with nothing to be third to, it reads as disabled.

danger-confirm.intent: The destructive action INSIDE its own confirmation dialogue, where it is the thing that dialogue exists for.
danger-confirm.notes: The same action at a different rank, which is the point of two patterns. In the page the delete is tertiary; in the modal that asks about nothing else it is the primary and takes the solid fill. Rank is a property of the screen, not of the verb. It also keeps "one solid fill per viewport" exactly true rather than roughly true — the modal is its own viewport and the page behind it is covered.
donts: Never outside a confirmation. If there is no dialogue, the delete is `danger`.

outlined.intent: Any button whose border replaces its fill.
outlined.reason: Not because an outlined button is bad — it is a perfectly good secondary, and for a lighter archetype it is arguably the better one. Because this product already chose the FILLED secondary, and claude-4.md is explicit that having both on one screen creates a fourth level of hierarchy that no reader can rank: a filled neutral and an outline are the same weight, expressed two ways. The choice is per product, once, and this product made it. Reversing it means moving the secondary AND the destructive together, not adding one outline.

size.intent: Physical size. Orthogonal to emphasis — a secondary button can be small without becoming a different pattern.

medium.intent: The default, 44px from the multiplatform override. Adds no class, so most call sites name no size at all.

small.intent: Dense rows: an ingredient line, an inline action in a step.

card.intent: A bounded block of recipe content resting on the page: a recipe in a list, the ingredients, a note.
card.namespaceNote: The root class only. `card-body`, `card-title`, `card-text`, `card-header` and `card-img-top` are ANATOMY — the markup CoreUI requires — not variants, so no pattern produces them and claiming them would make the verifier report ordinary markup as unknown. `bg-body-tertiary` used to be claimed here as the one background utility a card could take; the pattern that needed it is forbidden below, and the utility went with it.

default.intent: The standard block, resting on the page and separated from it by a hairline.
dos: Let a photograph run to the edge of its own card, and no further.
donts: Never separate two cards with a shadow — this product carries hierarchy in tone.
Never give a card its own recessed tone. Excavation is spent on fields.

trajectory.when: the first recipe card that carries a photograph
trajectory.why: CoreUI's card is a generic container and the chosen form is a framed photo at a fixed ratio, which it has no expression for. Every card on the page is currently the library's shape with this product's colours.

sunken.intent: A recessed block inside a recipe: a tip, the cook's note, a utensils list.
sunken.reason: It was allowed until 0.9.0 and it was a third surface in a product whose composition lists two. The deeper reason is what excavation is FOR. claude-5.md: "escavação é quase sempre um nível só, e é local" — one level, and it belongs to the thing that receives content, which is a field. Once `$field-bg` is the sunken tone, a recessed card and a textarea are the same colour, and a reader has to work out which of the two boxes can be typed in. A note is not a hole in the page; it is a card whose CONTENT differs, and the handwriting face already says so.

field.intent: A form control for editing a recipe, an ingredient, or the search box.
field.namespaceNote: The control classes only. `form-label`, `form-text` and `form-check` are anatomy and are left unclaimed.

text.intent: Single-line or multi-line text: a recipe title, a step.

select.intent: A choice from a closed list: a category, a unit of measure.

check.intent: Ticking off an ingredient while cooking.

nav.intent: Moving between sections of one recipe, or between areas of the notebook.
nav.namespaceNote: The root plus the variant classes, ENUMERATED rather than excluded, and `rail`, which is this product own. `nav-item`, `nav-link` and `rail-link` are anatomy; a lookahead like `^nav-(?!bar)` would claim them and report every tab link as an unknown variant. `nav-justified` is enumerated because in this product it is not optional — the tabs are always equal-width, so it is part of the pattern rather than a modifier of it.

tabs.intent: Sections within one recipe: ingredients, method, notes.
dos: Section-level navigation inside a single recipe.
Inactive labels one ink below the active one, so the chosen tab dominates instead of competing.
donts: Not for moving between recipes — that is a route, not a tab.
Never an accent border on the active tab. That is the focus ring.
Never a second tab design elsewhere in the product.
tabs.responsive: Below the tablet breakpoint these stack as headings in the flow; tabs sit at the top of a phone screen and compete with the header.

trajectory.why: The shape is now right and the responsive answer still is not: the responsive note below promises these stack as headings below the tablet breakpoint, and the markup does not yet do it. That is the remaining reason to own this component, and it is a layout reason rather than a colour one.
trajectory.form: stacked headings below the tablet breakpoint

tabs.notes: ONE TAB DESIGN, and for a while the product had two. An underline tab and an enclosed tab are the same component drawn two ways, and a design system tolerates two patterns for "selected" across a whole product — with a rule saying when each applies — never two for one component. The enclosed one is official. Its active state also used to be an ACCENT border, which is the vocabulary of a focus ring: a keyboard user could not distinguish selected from focused, which is an accessibility failure rather than a preference. The accent outline is now reserved for focus, and  fails the build if any component takes it back. What carries the state instead is what a closed, contiguous set should use — the chosen tab comes FORWARD out of the track, neutral surface and neutral edge, with position doing the rest.

rail.intent: Moving between areas of the notebook: the caderno itself, exploring, writing, the shopping list.
rail.notes: CoreUI has a sidebar and it is an application chrome component — collapsible, with its own brand block, its own toggler and its own surface. This product wants four links against a hairline. `own` rather than `styled` because there is no library component underneath: it is a flex column built from tokens, and the whole of it is about forty lines in `app.css`. It spends NO rung, which is the decision the ledger is really recording — see the composition `donts`. THE ACTIVE ITEM WAS A WASHED ACCENT AND IT WAS THE WORST THING ON THE PAGE. Three causes compounded, and the order matters because only the first is about colour: a nav is a closed contiguous set and should never have spent accent at all; the rail sits on the PAGE while the cards sit a rung above it, so a fill calibrated for a card had almost no separation left out here (a rung is a distance from a surface, not a property of a component); and audit-wash measures 146 degrees of hue between pigment and paper, where a pale patch reads as a stain rather than a tint. The fill now sinks two neutral rungs, and the accent returns as a 3px solid bar — which is also the cheaper accent, because the budget is area multiplied by chroma and a washed row paints far more than a bar at full strength.
dos: A hairline between the rail and the content, in the divider tone.
The current destination sinks TWO NEUTRAL RUNGS and takes a 3px solid accent bar. Not a washed accent — see the donts.
Weight on the active label, always. A state carried by tone alone is a state some readers do not receive.
donts: Never a surface tone of its own. That would be the third rung, and this product has two.

Never a washed accent on the active item. A nav is a CLOSED, CONTIGUOUS set — position already says which one is chosen, so the accent buys nothing the layout had not said. It is the same argument that keeps a segmented control neutral.
Never a solid accent fill on the active item either. The solid belongs to the one action the screen exists for.
rail.responsive: Below the tablet breakpoint it becomes a scrolling row above the content, not a hamburger. A phone is narrower, not denser, so the rail moves rather than compacts.

modal.intent: A dialog that blocks until answered. In this product it exists for one job.
modal.namespaceNote: The root class only. `modal-dialog`, `modal-content`, `modal-header`, `modal-body` and `modal-footer` are the anatomy CoreUI requires; `modal-backdrop` is generated by the library at runtime.

confirmation.intent: Confirming something that cannot be undone: deleting a saved recipe.
dos: Action-oriented register in the body text, per voiceExceptions — nobody wants charm from the thing that just deleted a recipe.
donts: Not for anything reversible. A toast with undo is the pattern for that, and this product has not needed one yet.

badge.intent: A read-only label on a recipe: a time, a category, a difficulty.
badge.namespaceNote: `badge` plus the two utilities that can act as its fill. `bg-body-secondary` is claimed because on a badge it IS the variant; `text-bg-*` is claimed so the refusal below can catch it.

neutral.intent: The only badge this product has. A label is not a status, and it is not an action either.
neutral.notes: The library's own badge, rendering as a paper chip with no product CSS. Three token decisions get it there: the adapter binds `--cui-badge-color` and `--cui-badge-border-radius`, which CoreUI exposes and nobody had bound; the adapter points `--cui-secondary-bg-rgb` at `bg-neutral-subtle`; and the entry configures layer 3 with `$badge-fg: fg-muted`. CoreUI hardcodes `--cui-badge-color: #fff` inside the rule, which is why it looked untokenisable — a literal in a declaration is still beatable by the same variable at a later layer. A TRAJECTORY WAS REMOVED HERE IN 0.9.0 rather than completed. It read "promote this to a removable chip when a label has to become interactive", and it was blocked pending a ledger discussion. The discussion happened and the answer was that a label never becomes interactive: a badge reports what the content IS, a chip holds what the reader CHOSE, and they are two components because they are two meanings. `chip/filter` was added beside this instead. The badge stays what it is — read-only, adequate, and not stretching anywhere.

status-coloured.intent: A badge carrying a status colour, or the library's own badge classes.
status-coloured.reason: A status colour reports an outcome. A cooking time is not an outcome, and a green 30-minute badge teaches readers that green means nothing here. The whole `text-bg-*` family is refused for a second reason that no token can fix: every one of them declares `color: #fff !important` in the rule itself, so the ink cannot follow a theme. That is a real limit of the library, and a ledger is the right place to record it rather than fight it.

chip.intent: A filter the reader turns on and off. Not a badge and not a button: a badge is a label the content carries, a button performs an action, and a chip holds a CHOICE that stays held.
chip.namespaceNote: The root plus its variants. `chip-icon`, `chip-img` and `chip-remove` are anatomy and are claimed by this regex, which is a known cost: CoreUI names anatomy and variants alike. The alternative was an exclusion lookahead, and the refusal below needs to be able to catch eight colour variants by name, so enumeration wins.

filter.intent: Narrowing the notebook to one marker, ON THE PAGE: bolos, salgados, da vó.
filter.notes: CoreUI is the reason this ledger can have a chip at all — the only library of the ten here that ships a real selectable one, and the adapter binds every one of its variables to layer 3. NO BORDER: the resting fill is RUNG 3, which is the rung the ladder reserves for an element at rest, and that tone is the whole boundary. It pointed at bg-surface until 0.9.0 — a SURFACE LEVEL, the tone a card is made of — so a chip on the page measured a lightness difference of 0.015 and a chip inside a card vanished outright. The fix was the fill, not a border; see filter-on-surface for the case where a border IS the answer. SELECTED IS WASHED ACCENT, and that default was wrong too: bg-selected aliases onto the accent family in this school, so every ticked chip came out a full-strength block.
dos: Ticked chips sit two rungs BELOW the resting ones — darker, never lighter. In an elevated model a chosen thing that recedes is the one direction the eye reads as wrong.
aria-pressed on every one. The visual state is a tone, and a tone is not announced.
Inside a card, put data-surface="surface" on the container and change nothing else.
donts: Never a border, at rest or when chosen. An accent edge is the focus ring; a neutral edge is a second mechanism for a boundary the fill already drew.
Never as a label. A read-only tag is badge/neutral.

status-coloured.intent: A chip carrying a theme colour rather than the accent.
status-coloured.reason: The same refusal as the badge and the button, and the strongest of the three: a chip is already the one element allowed to take the accent when chosen, so a chip in six other colours empties the accent of the only meaning it has. This product has one pigment; a green chip would be the second.

filter-on-surface.intent: The same filter, sitting on a card or any surface already at rung 3.
filter-on-surface.reason: IT WAS A WORKAROUND FOR A BUG, and the bug is fixed. The outlined chip existed because a chip inside a card resolved to the same tone as the card — its fill was calibrated against the PAGE and nothing rescoped it on the way in — so a border was added to make it visible. That border was not a decision, it was a bandage. Surface contexts now shift every rung by the distance between the two grounds, so the ordinary filled chip works in both places with different values resolved automatically. What is left is what should have been there: one chip design, two states, both fills. The clue that it was always wrong: the product had seven colours inside a component that needs four.
